cells.tense: You are here at this shared table with the pen in your hand, sorting the version that holds from the one that only sounds good.
cells.ask: At your next meal with your people, bring up one thing your household actually does and ask what it used to be, before saying what you think.
cells.core:
You can see what your people actually live by, and you can see the story they keep telling about themselves. Those two are not the same, and the difference is plain to you. That is useful work, and it is running now.

It shows up quietly — in what gets repeated, what gets let go, which old habit you keep and which one you stop passing down. That sorting happens whether anyone names it or not. The risk is that your own judgment gets spent pleasing the room or keeping the peace. When that happens the group loses its one honest reading. Say the thing before the meal ends, in your own words, and let it stand in the air.

cells.tense: You are building tomorrow's case for what is true here before the person in front of you has finished their sentence.
cells.ask: Say the one sentence you want the room to carry, then stop — let an hour pass before you add the qualifications or the examples.
cells.core:
You are preparing the argument before anyone asked for it. The better version of the story is already put together in your head while the person across from you is still talking, and you are three steps ahead of the room.

The habit is not a bad one in itself — it is the same practice that lets you sort true from false in the first place. But pushed forward, it turns a living conversation into a briefing, and the shared thing stops being shared. The work here is to let what you know sit still. Finish your sentence and go quiet. The room can carry one clear line and then breathe. What comes after that belongs to the people in it, not to your preparation for them.

cells.tense: You were on that chair where saying what you saw meant something, and your body still braces when the moment comes to speak.
cells.ask: Spend one honest hour with what your group is actually doing — the mistake, the real gesture — before you ask anyone to take your read seriously.
cells.core:
When this is going well, the sorting and the saying happen in the same breath. You notice the difference between what the group practices and what it claims, and then you say it — plainly, to the people in the room, while it still matters. The table gets your reading and keeps moving. Nothing is lost in the gap.

What is happening instead: the sorting stays inside. You can tell what matters from what doesn't, exactly and without asking permission, and the telling stops at the edge of the room. There is something you hold back. Maybe saying it once went poorly, and since then the offering has stayed close to the chest. The moment of handing it over — the half-second when you decide whether the table gets to hear it — is where the line goes quiet. The people around you are short of exactly this.
cells.sheetLine: You can tell, and the telling keeps stopping at your own edge.
cells.verb: Honing — the private daily work of telling what actually holds from what only sounds right.
cells.place: In the shared thing — the table, the room, the repeating story a group hands forward.

cells.tense: The choosing is already in your daily acts — what you repeat and what you let go — and you talk about it as though the group were doing it through you.
cells.ask: At the next gathering, say out loud one distinction you have been making in how your people do things and have been calling it the way it has been done.
cells.core:
You already shape what the group carries. It shows in which habits you reinforce, which jokes you let die, which old story you keep telling at the yearly table. The work is happening. What is missing is that you describe it as the group doing it on its own, or as if it moves through you without your say.

No one is asking for a new invention. But a handed-over thing that no one has claimed cannot be handed further, and the next person who needs the distinction will not find it. The move is small and it is out loud. Name one of them as yours.
cells.sheetLine: You are already choosing what your people keep.
cells.verb: Honing — the private daily work of telling what actually holds from what only sounds right.

attempts.check: The only unsupported claim in my read is the Too Little cell's 'you saw it happen once, up close' — the record permits locating the person behind the present but not saying what happened there; I've kept it as a question rather than a statement of fact. A reader could reasonably say 'it didn't happen once, it's been happening every week for years, and nobody cared' — the ask (give one honest hour of attention before asking to be taken seriously again) still works if I'm wrong about the single event. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'You've already been holding the line on what's true — the room just doesn't know it yet,' because it flatters the writer with an insider's view of what the person is 'really' doing. Fixed: the Unacknowledged cell now describes what someone else in the room sees, not what the person is secretly doing.
